alt: Paper 1 has two 25-mark sections, each on an unseen text of about 550 to 750 words. Question 1(a), 10 marks, is a 150 to 200 word directed response (AO1, AO2); Question 1(b), 15 marks, compares it with the original (AO1, AO3); Question 2, 25 marks, comments on the form, structure and language of a second text (AO1, AO3).
caption: Question 1(b) carries more marks than 1(a), so plan the comparison while you write.

alt: The first pass reads for gist and situation: form, writer, audience and purpose. The second pass, with a pen, marks shifts in tone, time or focus, and sentence pattern. Before annotating, state the text's form, audience and purpose in one sentence.
caption: Establish form, audience and purpose before annotating features.

after: ## Family 2: analysing and writing about effects
alt: Second-person address, present tense and short imperatives in one paragraph combine into a single effect: urgency directed at the reader. Below, examples of overall style judgements, such as "detached and clinical", with the reminder that a judgement needs examples and examples need a judgement.
caption: Show features combining into one effect, and prove a stated overall style.

alt: Five steps: select the smallest piece of text that carries the effect, embed it in your own sentence, link it with a precise analytical verb, interpret it for this reader and context, and integrate it into your overall reading. Eight analytical verbs are offered instead of "shows".
caption: Select, embed, link, interpret, integrate: five skills that form one process.

alt: A weak answer quotes a whole clause and says it "shows the writer is angry". The strong version names the adverbial "once again", explains that it turns a single decision into a pattern, and links this to the article's wider strategy of presenting residents as long-suffering and officials as indifferent.
caption: Select two words, name the feature, explain the effect and link it to the argument.

alt: Writing in the same style keeps the source's features (sentence types, register, person, tense, devices) but not its words. Writing in a different style keeps the content but changes the style to fit a new form, purpose and audience, a transformation rather than a paraphrase.
caption: Same style borrows features; different style keeps content and transforms the form.

after: ## Worked example: same content, different style
alt: The lesson's reflective column about a library's last hour is compared with a website notice about new evening hours on five points: purpose, structure, sentence style, devices and attitude to the quiet. The column evokes a mood with sensory detail and a cumulative final clause; the notice informs with a headline, dates first and short declaratives.
caption: A 1(b) comparison works point by point and explains each difference through audience and purpose.
